Q: Time-filtered query working on sum(rate(..)), but not on sum by (label) (rate(..)) A:

VictoriaMetrics and Prometheus match time series with the same sets of labels on the left and the right side of the and operator (or any other binary operator ).

In the case above when the sum() is used without any grouping by labels, then the result of this sum() has zero labels. It matches the result of hour() ... on the right side of and - it also has zero labels. So the query works as expected.

When the sum() contains grouping by labels via by (...), then it returns results with these labels. These results do not match the single result on the right side of and, which has zero labels. That's why the query unexpectedly returns nothing.

Use on() or ignoring() modifiers for changing the subset of labels to use during matching of time series on the left and the right sides of and. In your case it is enough to add on() after the and in order to reduce the set of labels to match to an empty set:

with (
    filter = {resource="cpu_time", database_name="main_db"},
    metric = runtime_stats_microseconds_total{filter},
    current = metric[5m]
)
sum by (labelname) (rate(current)) and on() hour() >=6 <=18

Alternatively you can use ignoring(label_name) modifier.

See these docs for more details on how Prometheus and VictoriaMetrics match time series when executing binary operators such as and.

Q: Python: lil_matrix vs csr_matrix in extremely large sparse matrices A:

I would like to add to Akavall's answer and gerowam's comment, by illustrating how the sizes of these two sparse matrix formats depend on their specific contents.

Consider an n-by-n matrix. Its representation as lil_matrix contains arrays lil_matrix.rows and lil_matrix.data. rows is an array of n lists, each holding the indices of non-zero entries of a row. data is of the same shape as rows, and stores the specific non-zero entries of each row.

csr_matrix, on the other hand, stores non-zero entries in a 1D array csr_matrix.data. csr_matrix.indices stores the column indices of the entries of data, and csr_matrix.indptr stores the locations in data where one row ends and the next row begins.

This quick experiment can illustrate the sizes of lil_matrix and csr_matrix depending on how sparse the matrices are:

import numpy as np
import scipy.sparse as sp
import sys

def lil_size(mat):
    total = 0
    for row_vals, row_idxs in zip(mat.data, mat.rows):
        total += sys.getsizeof(row_vals)
        total += sys.getsizeof(row_idxs)
        total += sum(sys.getsizeof(v) for v in row_vals)
        total += sum(sys.getsizeof(i) for i in row_idxs)
    return total

def csr_size(mat):
    total = mat.data.nbytes + mat.indices.nbytes + mat.indptr.nbytes
    return total

def lil_vs_csr_vs_dense(rng, n, num_nonzero):
    """
    Prints the sizes of `lil_matrix`, `csr_matrix`, and dense array representations of an `n`-by-`n` sparse matrix with `num_nonzero` non-zero entries.
    """
    # Randomly generate `num_nonzero` pairs of indices and `num_nonzero`
    # non-zero entries
    indices = rng.integers(0, n, (num_nonzero, 2))
    entries = rng.integers(0, 10, num_nonzero)

    # Build lil_matrix with non-zero entries as given above
    lil_mat = sp.lil_matrix((n, n))
    for i in range(num_nonzero):
        j, k = indices[i]
        entry = entries[i]
        lil_mat[j, k] += entry

    # Convert lil_matrix to csr_matrix and dense array
    csr_mat = lil_mat.tocsr()
    dense_mat = lil_mat.toarray()

    # Print sizes of the three representations
    indent_print = lambda x: print(f"    {x}")
    indent_print_each = lambda x_arr: [indent_print(x) for x in x_arr]
    print(
        f"Sizes of {n}-by-{n} lil_matrix, csr_matrix, and dense array with\n"
        + f"{f"roughly {num_nonzero} non-zero" if num_nonzero != 0 else "zero"} "
        + "entries:"
    )
    indent_print_each((lil_size(lil_mat), csr_size(csr_mat), dense_mat.nbytes))
    print()


n = 10**3
rng = np.random.default_rng()
for num_nonzero in (0, n, 10 * n, 100 * n):
    lil_vs_csr_vs_dense(rng, n, num_nonzero)

Q: How do I get the .exe name of a C# console application? A:

For .NET 6 Console App (or later)

    Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly().Location

will give you the full path of the executing assembly DLL.

To get the executable name you can replace the extension:

string dllPath = Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly().Location;
string exePath = $"{Path.GetFileNameWithoutExtension(dllPath)}.exe";
FileVersionInfo fvi = FileVersionInfo.GetVersionInfo(exePath);

References

  • Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly()

  • Assembly.Location

  • FileVersionInfo.GetVersionInfo()

Q: Can a dictation text editor be built in MS Visual C#? A:

You can use the SpeechRecognizer class in System.Speech.

If you handle the SpeechRecognized event the text is in e.Result.Text.
